catalog_quote: [Swadesh 1946: 114] The sounds represented by the remaining symbols are fairly typical and may be passed over except to mention that e° represents a very open sound, close to the English vowel in cat. Accent is a purely mechanical function of phrase rhythm: phrases are normally accented on the last syllable. The Atakapa material includes forms from three dialects: the bulk is Western Atakapa (shown as At. or W.) recorded in 1885 by Gatschet with a few later additions by Swanton ... [p. 115] Evidently reflecting the accentual weakness of open, non-final syllables, are a number of cases in which such syllables are found with and without initial h; thus, hipa, ipa husband. In giving words of this type, we show only the writing with h. Likewise in open, non-final syllables, we find a few cases of variant vowel writing: yemoy, yimop cheap; temak, timak knee ... [Gatschet & Swanton 1932: 6] A…

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every quoted passage is verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated pages (only the Kaufman 2014 locator should read pp. 77-78, not p. 75). The classification PHRASAL/phrase rests on Swadesh 1946, a comparative phonology article reinterpreting Gatschet's 1885 notes, with the accent claim a single hedged sentence ('normally') in a paragraph covering both Atakapa and Chitimacha. Against Glottolog's list, the best available description is Kimball 2022 (UNP reference grammar, Phonology ch. pp. 1-18), which we do not hold and could not download (JSTOR/MUSE bot walls; no open copy found via CrossRef/OpenLibrary/Glottolog; Two concrete signals make the classification vulnerable rather than merely thin: (i) Kimball's title orthography marks accent on a non-final syllable (Yukhíti Kóy), implying he assigns word-level

sources.note: Tone is not mentioned anywhere. The only prosodic content: Gatschet & Swanton's ka′kha-u 'sun' vs kakau′ 'water' may show 'a difference in stress' (initial vs final), and the conclusion states that questions of 'phonetics, phonology, and stress' are all but impossible to resolve for this dormant, relative-less language.

tone.quote: [p. 77, note to Line 13] In his dictionary, however, ‘sun’ is ka′kha-u (1932: 178) and ‘water’ is kakau′ (1932: 180), indicating an apparent difference in the phonetic quality of the middle k (aspirated?) and possibly a difference in stress (first syllable stress in the former and final syllable stress in the latter). [p. 78, sec. Conclusion] Needless to say, this makes solving certain problems, such as those related to phonetics, phonology, and stress, all but impossible to solve.

sources.note: The only modern reference grammar (Glottolog's sole listed by Glottolog as a grammar entry, 318 pp) with an 18-page phonology chapter; our PHRASAL coding rests on one 1946 sentence in a joint Atakapa-Chitimacha paragraph, and Kimball's accent-marked orthography (Yukhíti, non-final accent) hints at a word-level accent analysis that could overturn or refine PHRASAL/phrase.
